lesson_title: How Net Income Flows Into Equity
question_or_heading: Profit doesn't just vanish
option_a: Net income from the income statement flows directly into the balance sheet, adding to retained earnings — one of the clearest links between the two statements.

lesson_title: How Net Income Flows Into Equity
question_or_heading: Dividends reduce that flow
option_a: If the company pays dividends, that portion of net income leaves retained earnings again — only the retained (kept) portion actually builds up equity.

lesson_title: How Net Income Flows Into Equity
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Net income flows from the income statement into retained earnings on the balance sheet, reduced by any dividends paid out.

lesson_title: How Net Income Flows Into Equity
question_or_heading: A company starts the year with ₹50,00,000 in retained earnings, earns ₹10,00,000 in net income, and pays ₹3,00,000 in dividends. What is its retained earnings at year end?
hint: Ending Retained Earnings = Beginning + Net Income − Dividends.
explanation: ₹50,00,000 + ₹10,00,000 − ₹3,00,000 = ₹57,00,000 — the net income that wasn't paid out as dividends adds to retained earnings.

lesson_title: How Net Income Flows Into Equity
question_or_heading: Which balance sheet line item is most directly connected to the income statement's net income figure?
option_a: Cash
option_b: Retained earnings (part of equity)
option_c: Accounts payable
option_d: Inventory
hint: Which equity component builds up specifically from accumulated profit?
explanation: Retained earnings is literally the running total of profit the company has kept over its history — the direct landing spot for each period's net income.

lesson_title: How Net Income Flows Into Equity
question_or_heading: A company that pays out 100% of its net income as dividends would see no change to its retained earnings that period.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: If none of the profit is retained, what's left to add to retained earnings?
explanation: With the entire net income distributed as dividends, there's nothing left over to add — retained earnings stays flat that period.

lesson_title: How Net Income Flows Into Equity
question_or_heading: A company reports a net LOSS of ₹5,00,000 for the year (negative net income). What happens to retained earnings?
option_a: It increases by ₹5,00,000
option_b: It decreases by ₹5,00,000, since a net loss reduces accumulated profit
option_c: It's completely unaffected by losses
option_d: Losses only affect the cash flow statement
hint: Does the same formula (Beginning + Net Income − Dividends) work when net income is negative?
explanation: A net loss flows through the same link, just in the negative direction — reducing retained earnings, since accumulated profit shrinks when the company loses money.

lesson_title: How Net Income Flows Into Equity
question_or_heading: Why is this link between net income and retained earnings considered one of the clearest examples of how the three financial statements connect?
option_a: Because it's the only connection between any two statements
option_b: Because it directly shows the income statement's bottom-line result flowing into and permanently changing a specific balance sheet line item
option_c: Because retained earnings has nothing to do with net income
option_d: Because this link only applies to companies that never pay dividends
hint: What makes this particular link such a clean, direct illustration of statement interconnection?
explanation: This is about as direct a link as it gets: a period's bottom-line result on the income statement flows straight into a specific, trackable balance sheet line — making it a natural first example of how the statements connect.

lesson_title: How Capex Flows Into the Balance Sheet
question_or_heading: Capex builds up fixed assets
option_a: Capital expenditures (capex) — cash spent on long-term assets, tracked in investing cash flow — directly increases the property, plant & equipment line on the balance sheet.

lesson_title: How Capex Flows Into the Balance Sheet
question_or_heading: Cash goes down as the asset goes up
option_a: When a company pays cash for new equipment, cash (an asset) decreases while property/equipment (another asset) increases by roughly the same amount — assets shift form, they don't just disappear.

lesson_title: How Capex Flows Into the Balance Sheet
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Capital expenditures reduce cash and increase fixed assets on the balance sheet, in roughly matching amounts — the same transaction appears in two places.

lesson_title: How Capex Flows Into the Balance Sheet
question_or_heading: A company spends ₹20,00,000 cash to build a new warehouse. What happens to its balance sheet?
option_a: Total assets increase by ₹20,00,000
option_b: Cash decreases by ₹20,00,000 while property/equipment increases by ₹20,00,000 — total assets stay roughly the same
option_c: Total assets decrease by ₹20,00,000
option_d: Only liabilities are affected
hint: Recall the balance sheet capstone lesson's example of buying equipment with cash — is this creating new assets, or converting one into another?
explanation: Just like buying equipment outright with cash, building a warehouse converts one asset (cash) into another (fixed assets) — total assets stay roughly balanced, just redistributed.

lesson_title: How Capex Flows Into the Balance Sheet
question_or_heading: Where does the cash spent on capex first appear on the cash flow statement, before it shows up as a new fixed asset on the balance sheet?
option_a: Operating cash flow
option_b: Investing cash flow, as a cash outflow
option_c: Financing cash flow
option_d: It never appears on the cash flow statement
hint: Recall which cash flow section captures spending on long-term assets.
explanation: Capex is a textbook investing activity — the cash flow statement records it as an outflow there, before that same spending shows up as a new fixed asset on the balance sheet.

lesson_title: How Capex Flows Into the Balance Sheet
question_or_heading: Capital expenditures immediately reduce net income by the full amount spent, in the same period.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Recall the depreciation lesson — is a large asset purchase expensed all at once, or spread over time?
explanation: Capex isn't expensed immediately — it becomes a balance sheet asset and gets expensed gradually over time through depreciation, exactly as covered in the cash flow statement unit.

lesson_title: How Capex Flows Into the Balance Sheet
question_or_heading: A company's fixed assets grow by ₹50,00,000 over the year, and its cash flow statement shows ₹50,00,000 in capex. What does this consistency confirm?
option_a: Nothing — these two numbers are unrelated
option_b: That the growth in fixed assets on the balance sheet is being properly explained by actual cash spending on the cash flow statement — the two statements are lining up as expected
option_c: That the company must have made an accounting error
option_d: That the company has stopped depreciating its assets
hint: Should these two figures from two different statements naturally match up, if nothing else changed?
explanation: Seeing capex on the cash flow statement match the growth in fixed assets on the balance sheet (before accounting for any depreciation in between) is a healthy sign the statements are internally consistent — a useful cross-check.

lesson_title: How Capex Flows Into the Balance Sheet
question_or_heading: Why is tracing a single transaction — like a capex purchase — across both the cash flow statement and balance sheet a valuable exercise for understanding financial statements?
option_a: It has no real value, since the statements are completely independent
option_b: It builds an intuitive sense of how the three statements form one connected system, rather than three unrelated documents
option_c: This exercise is only useful for auditors, never analysts
option_d: Capex is the only transaction that ever appears on more than one statement
hint: What deeper understanding does tracing one transaction across multiple statements build, that reading each statement in isolation wouldn't?
explanation: Tracing a single real transaction through multiple statements is exactly how the intuition that 'these are one connected system, not three separate documents' gets built — a foundational skill for the rest of this unit.

lesson_title: How Depreciation Links All Three Statements
question_or_heading: On the income statement: an expense
option_a: Depreciation reduces net income on the income statement, as the cost of a long-lived asset gets allocated across its useful life.

lesson_title: How Depreciation Links All Three Statements
question_or_heading: On the cash flow statement: added back
option_a: Since depreciation is non-cash, it gets added back to net income when computing operating cash flow — reversing its effect for cash purposes.

lesson_title: How Depreciation Links All Three Statements
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Depreciation reduces net income on the income statement, gets added back on the cash flow statement, and reduces the fixed asset balance on the balance sheet — touching all three.

lesson_title: How Depreciation Links All Three Statements
question_or_heading: On which statement does depreciation reduce the value of a fixed asset over time?
option_a: Income statement
option_b: Cash flow statement
option_c: Balance sheet, where accumulated depreciation reduces the net book value of the asset
option_d: It doesn't affect any statement directly
hint: Which statement tracks what an asset is currently 'worth' on the books?
explanation: On the balance sheet, accumulated depreciation steadily reduces a fixed asset's net book value, reflecting its use and aging over time.

lesson_title: How Depreciation Links All Three Statements
question_or_heading: Depreciation appears on all three financial statements. Which of these correctly matches depreciation's effect on EACH statement?
option_a: Increases net income; is subtracted on cash flow; increases fixed assets
option_b: Decreases net income; is added back on cash flow; decreases the fixed asset balance
option_c: Has no effect on any of the three statements
option_d: Only appears on the balance sheet, nowhere else
hint: Recall each statement's specific treatment from this unit and the previous one.
explanation: This is exactly depreciation's three-way footprint: reduces net income (income statement), gets added back to reconcile to real cash (cash flow statement), and steadily shrinks the fixed asset's book value (balance sheet).

lesson_title: How Depreciation Links All Three Statements
question_or_heading: Depreciation is a rare example of a single accounting concept that shows up meaningfully across all three main financial statements.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: How many of the three statements does this lesson show depreciation touching?
explanation: Depreciation is a great example precisely because it threads through all three: reducing profit, being added back for cash purposes, and reducing an asset's book value — a genuinely three-statement concept.

lesson_title: How Depreciation Links All Three Statements
question_or_heading: A company with very high depreciation charges would show which pattern, connecting all three statements?
option_a: Lower net income, lower operating cash flow, and a rapidly shrinking fixed asset balance
option_b: Lower net income (income statement), but higher operating cash flow relative to net income due to the add-back (cash flow statement), and a shrinking fixed asset balance over time (balance sheet)
option_c: No effect on any statement
option_d: Higher net income across all three statements
hint: Walk through each statement's specific effect one at a time, as covered in this lesson.
explanation: Putting the three effects together: net income is pulled down by the expense, cash flow is pulled back up relative to net income by the add-back, and the balance sheet's fixed assets steadily shrink — one concept, three connected effects.

lesson_title: How Depreciation Links All Three Statements
question_or_heading: Why is understanding depreciation's three-statement footprint particularly useful when building a financial model that links all three statements together?
option_a: It isn't useful — depreciation can be safely ignored in financial models
option_b: Getting depreciation's treatment right in each statement is exactly what keeps a 3-statement model internally consistent and properly linked
option_c: Financial models only ever use one statement at a time
option_d: Depreciation is calculated completely differently in a model than in real financial statements
hint: What happens to a 3-statement model's internal consistency if depreciation isn't threaded correctly through all three?
explanation: In a proper 3-statement model, depreciation has to flow correctly through all three statements simultaneously — getting this one concept right is a strong test of whether the whole model is properly linked, which is exactly why this lesson matters heading toward Unit 10's capstone.

lesson_title: How Debt Links the Balance Sheet & Cash Flow
question_or_heading: Borrowing shows up in two places at once
option_a: Taking on new debt increases cash (an asset) and increases a liability, both on the balance sheet — and shows up as a positive financing cash flow on the cash flow statement.

lesson_title: How Debt Links the Balance Sheet & Cash Flow
question_or_heading: Repaying debt reverses both
option_a: Paying down principal reduces cash and reduces the liability balance on the balance sheet, and appears as a negative financing cash flow.

lesson_title: How Debt Links the Balance Sheet & Cash Flow
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: New borrowing increases both cash and a liability, and shows as a positive financing cash flow; repayment reverses all three simultaneously.

lesson_title: How Debt Links the Balance Sheet & Cash Flow
question_or_heading: A company borrows ₹1,00,00,000 from a bank. Which of these correctly describes the combined effect?
option_a: Cash and liabilities both increase on the balance sheet; financing cash flow shows a positive ₹1,00,00,000
option_b: Only cash increases, with no effect on liabilities
option_c: Only liabilities increase, with no effect on cash
option_d: Equity increases by the full loan amount
hint: Recall the balance sheet equation lesson's loan example — does the balance sheet stay balanced when a company borrows?
explanation: Borrowing brings in cash (an asset) and creates a matching liability — keeping the balance sheet balanced — while the cash flow statement records the same event as a financing inflow.

lesson_title: How Debt Links the Balance Sheet & Cash Flow
question_or_heading: A company repays ₹20,00,000 of loan principal during the year. What happens on the balance sheet and cash flow statement together?
option_a: Cash and the loan liability both decrease; financing cash flow shows a negative ₹20,00,000
option_b: Cash increases while the liability stays the same
option_c: Nothing changes on either statement
option_d: Only the income statement is affected
hint: Is repaying a loan a mirror image of taking one out?
explanation: Repayment is simply the reverse of borrowing: cash and the liability both shrink on the balance sheet, matched by a negative financing outflow on the cash flow statement.

lesson_title: How Debt Links the Balance Sheet & Cash Flow
question_or_heading: Interest paid on a loan appears in the financing section of the cash flow statement, alongside principal repayments.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Recall the income statement's treatment of interest — does interest expense sit with financing decisions, or does its cash payment usually get grouped with operating activity?
explanation: Interest payments are typically classified within operating cash flow (reflecting the expense on the income statement), while it's specifically the loan's principal that moves through the financing section — a common point of confusion worth remembering.

lesson_title: How Debt Links the Balance Sheet & Cash Flow
question_or_heading: A company's total liabilities on the balance sheet grew by exactly the amount shown as 'new borrowing' in the financing section of its cash flow statement, with no repayments that year. What does this consistency demonstrate?
option_a: Nothing meaningful — coincidence
option_b: The balance sheet and cash flow statement are properly linked and internally consistent for this transaction, exactly as they should be
option_c: That the company made an error somewhere
option_d: That interest rates must have changed
hint: Should new borrowing on the cash flow statement match the corresponding rise in liabilities on the balance sheet?
explanation: Just as with the capex example earlier in this unit, seeing new borrowing on the cash flow statement match the corresponding rise in liabilities on the balance sheet confirms the two statements are properly, consistently linked.

lesson_title: How Debt Links the Balance Sheet & Cash Flow
question_or_heading: Why does tracing debt through both the balance sheet and cash flow statement matter for someone building a financial model?
option_a: It doesn't matter, since debt is a static, unchanging number in any model
option_b: A model needs to correctly roll the debt balance forward each period (balance sheet) while matching new borrowing or repayment exactly to the financing section (cash flow) — getting this wrong breaks the model's links
option_c: Debt only ever appears on the balance sheet in a proper model
option_d: Financial models never need to track cash flow and balance sheet items together
hint: What two things does a correctly built model need to keep synchronized regarding debt?
explanation: A properly linked 3-statement model needs the debt balance rolling forward correctly on the balance sheet while precisely matching new borrowing and repayments in the cash flow statement's financing section — exactly the kind of internal consistency this unit is building toward.

lesson_title: Working Capital: The Connective Tissue
question_or_heading: Living on the balance sheet, moving through cash flow
option_a: Receivables, inventory, and payables live as balance sheet line items, but their period-to-period CHANGES are what show up as adjustments on the cash flow statement.

lesson_title: Working Capital: The Connective Tissue
question_or_heading: The balance sheet holds the position; cash flow holds the movement
option_a: Think of the balance sheet as a snapshot of the working capital balance, and the cash flow statement as tracking how much that balance moved, and what that movement did to cash.

lesson_title: Working Capital: The Connective Tissue
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Working capital items sit on the balance sheet as balances, but their period-over-period changes are what flow through as adjustments on the cash flow statement.

lesson_title: Working Capital: The Connective Tissue
question_or_heading: A company's accounts receivable balance was ₹10,00,000 at the start of the year and ₹14,00,000 at the end. What figure would appear as a cash flow adjustment?
option_a: The full ₹14,00,000 ending balance
option_b: The ₹4,00,000 increase, subtracted as a use of cash
option_c: The ₹10,00,000 starting balance
option_d: Nothing — receivables never appear on the cash flow statement
hint: Is it the balance itself, or the CHANGE in the balance, that flows through to cash flow?
explanation: It's specifically the ₹4,00,000 change (the increase) that becomes the cash flow adjustment, not either of the balance sheet snapshot figures on their own.

lesson_title: Working Capital: The Connective Tissue
question_or_heading: Why does the cash flow statement care about the CHANGE in a working capital item, rather than its absolute balance?
option_a: Absolute balances are always more important than changes
option_b: Because it's the movement in the balance during the period that actually represents cash tied up or freed up that period — the balance itself is just a snapshot
option_c: Changes in working capital never actually affect cash
option_d: The cash flow statement ignores working capital entirely
hint: What actually represents a real cash effect during the period — a snapshot, or a movement?
explanation: A snapshot balance doesn't tell you what happened during the period — it's the movement (the change) that represents real cash tied up or released, which is exactly what the cash flow statement needs to capture.

lesson_title: Working Capital: The Connective Tissue
question_or_heading: If accounts payable stays exactly the same from the start to the end of the year, it would produce zero cash flow adjustment for that period.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: No change in the balance means no cash flow effect from that item this period — true or false?
explanation: With no change in the balance, there's nothing to adjust for — a flat payables balance means zero cash flow impact from that line item during the period.

lesson_title: Working Capital: The Connective Tissue
question_or_heading: An analyst wants to understand a company's working capital dynamics fully. Which combination of statements do they need?
option_a: The balance sheet alone is sufficient
option_b: The income statement alone is sufficient
option_c: Both the balance sheet (for the balances at each point in time) and the cash flow statement (for how those balances changed and what that did to cash) together
option_d: Neither statement is relevant to working capital
hint: Recall the 'snapshot vs. movement' framing from this lesson — does one statement alone capture the full picture?
explanation: Getting the full working capital picture requires both: the balance sheet's snapshots to know the levels, and the cash flow statement's adjustments to know how those levels moved and what that meant for cash.

lesson_title: Working Capital: The Connective Tissue
question_or_heading: Why is working capital described in this lesson as the 'connective tissue' between the balance sheet and the cash flow statement?
option_a: Because it's a made-up term with no real analytical meaning
option_b: Because it's a clear, concrete example of the exact same underlying business activity being represented differently — as a balance in one statement, and as a period-over-period change in the other
option_c: Because working capital never actually appears on either statement
option_d: Because it only connects the income statement to the balance sheet, not cash flow
hint: What does the phrase 'connective tissue' capture about how the same underlying reality shows up differently on two statements?
explanation: Working capital is a clean, concrete illustration of exactly what 'linked statements' means in practice — the same real business activity (cash tied up in receivables, say) showing up as a balance on one statement and a period-over-period change on another, tying the two together.

lesson_title: Building a Simple 3-Statement Flow
question_or_heading: Picture the whole loop
option_a: Net income (income statement) flows into retained earnings (balance sheet). Depreciation (income statement) gets added back (cash flow) and shrinks fixed assets (balance sheet). Cash flow's ending cash becomes the balance sheet's cash line.

lesson_title: Building a Simple 3-Statement Flow
question_or_heading: Ending cash is the final handshake
option_a: The cash flow statement's ending cash balance should exactly match the cash line item on that period's balance sheet — this is the ultimate consistency check across all three statements.

lesson_title: Building a Simple 3-Statement Flow
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: The cash flow statement's ending cash balance must exactly equal the cash balance reported on that period's balance sheet — the final proof the three statements are properly linked.

lesson_title: Building a Simple 3-Statement Flow
question_or_heading: A company's cash flow statement shows an ending cash balance of ₹75,00,000 for the year. What should that same figure equal on the balance sheet, if the statements are properly linked?
option_a: It should have no particular relationship to the balance sheet
option_b: The cash line item on that period's balance sheet should also show ₹75,00,000
option_c: It should equal total assets, not just cash
option_d: It should equal total liabilities
hint: What's the ultimate cross-check between the cash flow statement and the balance sheet, as described in the intro cards?
explanation: The ending cash balance from the cash flow statement is exactly the figure that should appear as 'cash' on that same period's balance sheet — this handshake is the clearest proof the statements are properly linked.

lesson_title: Building a Simple 3-Statement Flow
question_or_heading: If a 3-statement model's calculated ending cash balance doesn't match its own balance sheet's cash line, what does that most likely indicate?
option_a: This is completely normal and expected in every model
option_b: There's likely an error somewhere in how the statements are linked, since these two figures must match exactly in a correctly built model
option_c: The company must have made a real-world accounting mistake
option_d: This mismatch is irrelevant and can be ignored
hint: In a properly built model, is a mismatch here a sign everything's fine, or a sign to go find the bug?
explanation: Since these two figures are supposed to be identical by construction, a mismatch is one of the most reliable signals that there's a linking error somewhere in the model that needs to be tracked down.

lesson_title: Building a Simple 3-Statement Flow
question_or_heading: In a correctly built financial model, net income, depreciation, working capital changes, and debt all ultimately flow through to affect the same final cash balance.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Does this lesson describe all these pieces as separate and disconnected, or as parts of one connected flow?
explanation: Exactly as this lesson lays out, all of these pieces — net income, depreciation, working capital, debt — are threads in one connected flow that all ultimately determine the same final cash number.

lesson_title: Building a Simple 3-Statement Flow
question_or_heading: Why is 'does ending cash on the cash flow statement match cash on the balance sheet' considered such a powerful sanity check for a 3-statement model?
option_a: It isn't powerful — it's a purely cosmetic check with no real diagnostic value
option_b: Because it's the one number that only comes out right if every single link (net income, depreciation, working capital, debt) was built correctly — a single mismatch anywhere breaks it
option_c: Because these two numbers are unrelated and always happen to differ
option_d: Because this check only works for very small companies
hint: What does the fact that EVERY link in the model feeds into this one final number make it such a strong diagnostic?
explanation: Because literally every link in a 3-statement model — from net income through depreciation, working capital, and debt — ultimately feeds into that single ending cash figure, getting it to match is a genuinely powerful, all-encompassing check that everything upstream was built correctly.

lesson_title: Building a Simple 3-Statement Flow
question_or_heading: This lesson sets up the unit's capstone: tracing a single transaction through all three statements. Why is tracing ONE transaction, rather than building a whole model, a good way to build this skill first?
option_a: It isn't a good way — you should always start with a full model
option_b: Following one transaction's complete path lets you see, in detail, exactly how a single event ripples through all three statements, before tackling the complexity of everything happening at once
option_c: Single transactions never actually affect more than one statement
option_d: This approach is only useful for auditors, not analysts
hint: What's easier to follow in detail — one transaction's full ripple effect, or everything happening across a whole model at once?
explanation: Following a single transaction's complete path across all three statements, in detail, builds the intuition needed before tackling the fuller complexity of a real model where many transactions are happening simultaneously — exactly the sequencing this unit is building toward its capstone.

lesson_title: What Happens When a Company Buys Inventory
question_or_heading: On credit, at first
option_a: When a company buys ₹5,00,000 of inventory on credit from a supplier, inventory (an asset) rises by ₹5,00,000, and accounts payable (a liability) rises by the same amount — the balance sheet stays balanced.

lesson_title: What Happens When a Company Buys Inventory
question_or_heading: No income statement impact yet
option_a: Buying inventory doesn't hit the income statement at all — that only happens later, when the inventory is actually sold, and its cost becomes part of COGS.

lesson_title: What Happens When a Company Buys Inventory
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Buying inventory on credit increases both inventory and accounts payable on the balance sheet — with no income statement effect until that inventory is later sold.

lesson_title: What Happens When a Company Buys Inventory
question_or_heading: A company buys ₹8,00,000 of raw materials on credit (not yet paid for). What happens to its balance sheet?
option_a: Inventory increases by ₹8,00,000; accounts payable increases by ₹8,00,000
option_b: Cash decreases by ₹8,00,000; inventory increases by ₹8,00,000
option_c: Only the income statement is affected, not the balance sheet
option_d: Nothing changes until the materials are paid for
hint: Is this purchase for cash, or on credit — and what liability does buying on credit create?
explanation: Buying on credit means no cash changes hands yet — instead, inventory rises (a new asset) and accounts payable rises by the same amount (the new obligation to the supplier), keeping the balance sheet balanced.

lesson_title: What Happens When a Company Buys Inventory
question_or_heading: When does the cost of purchased inventory typically hit the income statement as an expense (COGS)?
option_a: Immediately, the moment the inventory is purchased
option_b: Only later, when that inventory is actually sold to a customer
option_c: Inventory purchases never appear on the income statement
option_d: At the exact midpoint between purchase and sale, always
hint: Recall the intro card's explicit statement about timing.
explanation: Inventory sits on the balance sheet as an asset until it's actually sold — only at that point does its cost move to the income statement as cost of goods sold.

lesson_title: What Happens When a Company Buys Inventory
question_or_heading: Buying inventory on credit immediately reduces a company's reported net income for that period.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Does this transaction touch the income statement at all, based on the intro cards?
explanation: As the intro cards explained, buying inventory has no income statement effect at the time of purchase — net income is untouched until that inventory is later sold.

lesson_title: What Happens When a Company Buys Inventory
question_or_heading: A company pays CASH (not credit) for ₹3,00,000 of inventory. How does this differ from buying on credit, in terms of balance sheet impact?
option_a: There's no difference at all between the two scenarios
option_b: Cash decreases by ₹3,00,000 and inventory increases by ₹3,00,000 — one asset converts to another, with no new liability created, unlike the credit purchase
option_c: Buying with cash creates a liability, while credit purchases don't
option_d: Buying with cash always appears on the income statement immediately
hint: Compare this to the u7l2 capex example — is this converting one asset into another, or creating a new liability?
explanation: Just like the capex example, paying cash simply converts one asset (cash) into another (inventory) — no new liability, unlike the credit-purchase version which creates a payable.

lesson_title: What Happens When a Company Buys Inventory
question_or_heading: Why is walking through this specific transaction — buying inventory on credit — a useful exercise for understanding statement linkages, even though it's 'just' one small transaction?
option_a: It isn't useful, since inventory purchases are too minor to matter
option_b: It clearly shows how a single real-world event can touch two balance sheet accounts simultaneously while leaving the income statement completely untouched — exactly the kind of precise tracing this unit is building toward
option_c: This transaction actually affects all three statements equally
option_d: Inventory purchases are always identical to capex purchases in every respect
hint: What specific pattern — two accounts moving, one statement untouched — does this example illustrate clearly?
explanation: This transaction is a clean, small-scale illustration of exactly the kind of precise, statement-by-statement tracing this unit has been building toward — showing two balance sheet accounts moving together while the income statement stays completely unaffected.

lesson_title: What Happens When a Company Takes a Loan
question_or_heading: Revisiting the full picture
option_a: Building on the earlier debt lesson: when a company takes a ₹50,00,000 loan, cash rises by ₹50,00,000, the loan liability rises by ₹50,00,000, and the cash flow statement shows a ₹50,00,000 financing inflow — all at once.

lesson_title: What Happens When a Company Takes a Loan
question_or_heading: Then, every period after: interest and repayment
option_a: Each period, interest expense reduces net income (income statement) and typically flows through operating cash flow, while principal repayment reduces both cash and the loan balance and flows through financing cash flow.

lesson_title: What Happens When a Company Takes a Loan
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Taking a loan hits the balance sheet and financing cash flow immediately; interest hits the income statement and operating cash flow each period after; principal repayment hits the balance sheet and financing cash flow again.

lesson_title: What Happens When a Company Takes a Loan
question_or_heading: In the FIRST period a company takes out a loan, which of these is affected?
option_a: Only the income statement
option_b: Cash and the loan liability on the balance sheet, plus a financing inflow on the cash flow statement — no income statement effect yet
option_c: Only the cash flow statement's operating section
option_d: Only equity, not any liability
hint: Recall this unit's earlier lesson on debt — what happens the moment a loan is taken out, before any interest has accrued?
explanation: Just as covered earlier in this unit, taking out a loan itself is a balance sheet and financing cash flow event — no income statement impact until interest starts accruing in later periods.

lesson_title: What Happens When a Company Takes a Loan
question_or_heading: In each period AFTER the loan is taken out, which statement does the interest expense on that loan primarily affect?
option_a: The balance sheet only
option_b: The income statement, reducing net income, and typically operating cash flow
option_c: Only the financing section of the cash flow statement
option_d: No statement is affected by ongoing interest
hint: Recall the debt-linking lesson's note about where interest payments are typically classified, versus principal.
explanation: Interest expense reduces net income on the income statement each period, and its cash payment is typically classified within operating cash flow — distinct from principal repayments, which run through financing.

lesson_title: What Happens When a Company Takes a Loan
question_or_heading: Both taking out a loan and later repaying its principal show up in the financing section of the cash flow statement — just with opposite signs.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Are borrowing and principal repayment mirror-image financing activities?
explanation: Exactly as covered in the earlier debt lesson, both events are financing activities — borrowing shows as a positive inflow, repayment as a negative outflow, mirror images of each other.

lesson_title: What Happens When a Company Takes a Loan
question_or_heading: A company takes out a loan in Year 1, then pays interest and partial principal in Year 2. Which statements are touched in Year 2 specifically?
option_a: No statements are affected in Year 2
option_b: The income statement (interest expense), the cash flow statement (interest in operating, principal repayment in financing), and the balance sheet (declining loan balance, declining cash)
option_c: Only the balance sheet is affected in Year 2
option_d: Only the cash flow statement is affected in Year 2
hint: Walk through interest's effect and principal's effect separately, across all relevant statements.
explanation: Year 2 activity touches all three statements simultaneously: interest reduces income statement profit and shows in operating cash flow, while principal repayment reduces both cash and the loan balance and shows in financing cash flow — a genuinely three-statement period.

lesson_title: What Happens When a Company Takes a Loan
question_or_heading: Why does a loan's full lifecycle — origination, ongoing interest, and eventual repayment — make such a good comprehensive example for understanding 3-statement linkages?
option_a: Because loans are simple, one-time events with no ongoing effects
option_b: Because it touches all three statements, but with DIFFERENT effects at different points in time — origination, ongoing interest, and repayment each interact with the statements differently
option_c: Because loans never actually appear on the income statement
option_d: Because this pattern is unique to companies with no other assets
hint: What makes a loan's full lifecycle a richer example than a single one-time transaction like the inventory purchase from the last lesson?
explanation: Unlike a single transaction like the inventory purchase, a loan's full lifecycle demonstrates DIFFERENT statement interactions at different points in time — origination, ongoing interest, and repayment — making it a genuinely comprehensive example of how a single financial decision ripples across all three statements over time.

lesson_title: Common Linking Mistakes
question_or_heading: Forgetting to add back depreciation
option_a: A common modeling mistake: correctly subtracting depreciation on the income statement, but forgetting to add it back on the cash flow statement — silently understating operating cash flow.

lesson_title: Common Linking Mistakes
question_or_heading: Double-counting working capital changes
option_a: Another frequent error: adjusting for a working capital change in the wrong direction (adding instead of subtracting, or vice versa) — which throws off the entire cash flow reconciliation.

lesson_title: Common Linking Mistakes
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: The most common 3-statement linking mistakes involve forgetting non-cash add-backs, getting the direction of a working capital adjustment backward, or letting ending cash quietly stop matching the balance sheet.

lesson_title: Common Linking Mistakes
question_or_heading: An analyst correctly subtracts depreciation on the income statement, but forgets to add it back when building the cash flow statement. What's the effect?
option_a: Operating cash flow will be overstated
option_b: Operating cash flow will be understated, since a non-cash expense wasn't reversed out
option_c: Net income will be affected instead
option_d: There's no effect on either statement
hint: If a non-cash expense that should be added back gets left out, does cash flow end up too high or too low?
explanation: Forgetting the depreciation add-back leaves operating cash flow artificially low — the model is still treating a non-cash expense as if it were a real cash outflow.

lesson_title: Common Linking Mistakes
question_or_heading: An analyst treats a growing accounts receivable balance as a SOURCE of cash (adding it) instead of a USE of cash (subtracting it). What's the effect on operating cash flow?
option_a: No effect at all
option_b: Operating cash flow will be significantly overstated, in the wrong direction from reality
option_c: Operating cash flow will be understated by the correct amount
option_d: This mistake self-corrects automatically
hint: Recall the working capital changes lesson — does growing receivables tie up cash, or free it up? What happens if that's flipped?
explanation: Since a growing receivables balance actually ties up cash, treating it backward as a source flips the adjustment's sign entirely — overstating operating cash flow, potentially by a large margin depending on the size of the change.

lesson_title: Common Linking Mistakes
question_or_heading: The 'ending cash matches the balance sheet' check from earlier in this unit is a reliable way to catch many of these common linking mistakes.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: If a mistake throws off any part of the flow, would that likely show up in the final ending cash figure?
explanation: Because virtually every linking error eventually distorts the cash flow calculation somewhere, the ending-cash-matches-balance-sheet check is exactly the kind of catch-all sanity check that tends to expose these common mistakes.

lesson_title: Common Linking Mistakes
question_or_heading: Why do mistakes in 3-statement linking often go unnoticed until the ending cash figures fail to match, rather than being obvious immediately?
option_a: Because these mistakes are always immediately obvious on sight
option_b: Because a single wrong sign or missed add-back can look like a perfectly reasonable number in isolation — it's only when checked against the cross-statement consistency requirement that the error surfaces
option_c: Because these mistakes never actually cause any real problems
option_d: Because the balance sheet is never affected by cash flow statement errors
hint: Would a single miscalculated line item necessarily look 'wrong' on its own, without a cross-check against another statement?
explanation: A single flipped sign or missed add-back can look entirely plausible sitting in isolation — it's specifically the discipline of cross-checking against another statement (like ending cash vs. the balance sheet) that reliably surfaces these errors.

lesson_title: Common Linking Mistakes
question_or_heading: Given everything in this unit, what's the single best habit for avoiding these common linking mistakes when building or reviewing a 3-statement model?
option_a: Never check your work, and trust the first calculation
option_b: Systematically trace how each transaction type should affect all three statements, and use the ending-cash-matches-balance-sheet check as a final, comprehensive sanity test
option_c: Only ever look at the income statement
option_d: Assume errors are rare enough not to be worth checking for
hint: What combination of habits — from earlier in this unit — best guards against these mistakes?
explanation: Combining the transaction-tracing discipline built throughout this unit with the comprehensive ending-cash check from earlier is exactly the best defense against these common mistakes — precisely the skill set the unit's capstone lesson will now put to the test.

lesson_title: Capstone: Tracing a Transaction Through All Three
question_or_heading: One transaction, three statements, no exceptions
option_a: Any real business transaction — however complex it seems — can be traced through its full effect on the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement, one line at a time.

lesson_title: Capstone: Tracing a Transaction Through All Three
question_or_heading: The discipline that makes it click
option_a: Ask three questions for any transaction: does it touch the income statement? Which balance sheet accounts change? Which cash flow section, if any, does it appear in?

lesson_title: Capstone: Tracing a Transaction Through All Three
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Tracing any transaction through all three statements means systematically asking what it does to the income statement, which balance sheet accounts move, and where (if anywhere) it appears on the cash flow statement.

lesson_title: Capstone: Tracing a Transaction Through All Three
question_or_heading: A company sells goods for ₹6,00,000 on credit (not yet collected). Which of these correctly traces the FULL effect across the statements?
option_a: Revenue rises ₹6,00,000 (income statement); accounts receivable rises ₹6,00,000 (balance sheet); no cash flow effect yet, since no cash was collected
option_b: Only the balance sheet is affected
option_c: Only the cash flow statement is affected, since no cash changed hands
option_d: Nothing happens until the customer actually pays
hint: Walk through the three questions from the second intro card, one at a time, for a credit sale.
explanation: A credit sale hits revenue immediately (income statement) and creates a receivable (balance sheet), but generates no cash flow yet — that only comes later, when the customer actually pays, exactly the kind of full trace this unit has built toward.

lesson_title: Capstone: Tracing a Transaction Through All Three
question_or_heading: A company pays ₹2,00,000 cash for this month's rent. Which of these correctly traces the effect?
option_a: Rent expense reduces net income (income statement); cash decreases (balance sheet); a ₹2,00,000 operating cash outflow (cash flow statement) — all three statements affected simultaneously
option_b: Only the income statement is affected
option_c: This transaction has no balance sheet impact
option_d: Rent payments never affect cash flow
hint: Apply the three-question framework: income statement, balance sheet, cash flow — does a simple cash rent payment touch all three at once?
explanation: A straightforward cash expense like rent is actually one of the cleanest three-statement transactions: it reduces profit, reduces cash, and shows up as an operating outflow — all in the very same period, unlike the delayed cash effect of a credit sale.

lesson_title: Capstone: Tracing a Transaction Through All Three
question_or_heading: Every business transaction necessarily affects all three financial statements equally, in the same period.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Recall the inventory purchase example from earlier in this unit — did that transaction touch all three statements, or just two, at the time it happened?
explanation: As the inventory-purchase-on-credit example showed earlier in this unit, some transactions only touch two of the three statements (or touch them at very different times) — not every transaction hits all three simultaneously.

lesson_title: Capstone: Tracing a Transaction Through All Three
question_or_heading: A company issues new shares for ₹40,00,000 cash. Trace this transaction correctly.
option_a: Cash increases ₹40,00,000 and equity (share capital) increases ₹40,00,000 on the balance sheet; a ₹40,00,000 financing inflow on the cash flow statement; no income statement effect
option_b: This increases net income directly
option_c: This only affects the cash flow statement, not the balance sheet
option_d: This transaction creates a new liability
hint: Is issuing shares a financing activity, an operating one, or something that touches the income statement at all?
explanation: Issuing shares is a pure financing and balance sheet event — new cash and new equity move together, reflected as a financing inflow, with zero effect on the income statement, since selling ownership stakes isn't 'earning' anything.

lesson_title: Capstone: Tracing a Transaction Through All Three
question_or_heading: Reflecting on this entire unit — linking net income to equity, capex, depreciation, debt, working capital, and now full transaction tracing — what capability have you actually built?
option_a: The ability to memorize a fixed list of transaction types and their effects
option_b: A transferable framework — the three-question habit of checking income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow effects — that can correctly trace ANY transaction, not just the specific examples covered here
option_c: The ability to predict a company's future stock price
option_d: No transferable skill — each transaction type must be memorized separately with no underlying pattern
hint: Is the real skill built here a memorized list, or a repeatable method that generalizes beyond the specific examples covered?
explanation: The real achievement of this unit isn't memorizing each specific example — it's internalizing the three-question framework (income statement? balance sheet? cash flow?) as a transferable habit that can correctly trace literally any transaction, setting up exactly the skills Unit 10's full diagnostic capstone will call on.
